entities.summary:
The Republican Party of the United States, founded in 1854 by anti-slavery activists and former Whig Party members, is one of the world's oldest major political parties and has governed the United States for more of its history than any other party. Abraham Lincoln, the first Republican president (1861-1865), preserved the Union and abolished slavery; subsequent Republican presidents shaped American industrial capitalism, foreign policy, and the conservative movement that defined 20th-century American politics.

The Republican Party emerged from the crisis over slavery's expansion: the Kansas-Nebraska Act (1854) opened previously closed territories to slavery, galvanizing Northern anti-slavery sentiment into a new political coalition. The party's 1860 platform opposing slavery's expansion triggered the Southern secession that led to the Civil War. Lincoln's presidency and the Reconstruction Amendments (13th, 14th, 15th) abolishing slavery and establishing Black citizenship were the party's founding achievements.

The party's 20th-century evolution from Lincoln's anti-slavery party to the conservative movement — through Theodore Roosevelt's progressivism, Eisenhower's moderation, Nixon's Southern Strategy, Reagan's conservative revolution, and Trump's nationalist populism — represents one of political history's most complete ideological transformations. The Republican Party dominated the presidency from 1860-1932 (broken only by Wilson), then the conservative coalition from 1968 onward, making it the definitive governing party of the world's most powerful nation for extended periods.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Republican Party's abolition of American slavery under Lincoln — and its subsequent 160-year evolution into American conservatism — makes it the party most responsible for both America's defining moral achievement and its ongoing partisan divisions.
